t: The Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 came into force on:
e: The 1988 Act, which repealed the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939, was brought into force on 1 July 1989. The 1939 Act's compulsory insurance chapter had become effective on 1 July 1946.

t: In the United Kingdom, compulsory third party motor insurance was first introduced by:
e: The Road Traffic Act, 1930 made insurance against third party death and bodily injury compulsory in the UK, and Indian legislation of 1939 followed the same model.

t: The Declined Risk Pool for commercial vehicle third party business, which replaced the IMTPIP, commenced on:
e: The Declined Risk Pool began on 1 April 2012 for standalone commercial vehicle liability business that insurers did not wish to retain, with pool losses shared among insurers. The IMTPIP was dismantled with effect from 31 March 2012.

topic: Motor Vehicles Act and Legal Framework
t: Under Section 147 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, which of the following liabilities MUST be covered by an insurance policy?
o: Damage to the insured vehicle by accident
Personal accident benefit to passengers in a private car
Death of or bodily injury to any person (including owner of goods carried) and damage to third party property caused by use of the vehicle in a public place
e: Section 147 prescribes the minimum cover: liability for death or bodily injury to any person, including the owner of goods or his representative carried in the vehicle, and damage to property of a third party, plus WC Act liability to employees. Own damage and passenger PA are optional.

topic: Motor Vehicles Act and Legal Framework
t: Under the amended Section 164 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, no-fault compensation for grievous hurt is:
e: Section 164 fixes ₹5 lakh for death and ₹2.5 lakh for grievous hurt, payable without proof of negligence. A claimant who accepts this cannot also pursue a fault-based claim under Section 166 for the same accident.

topic: Motor Vehicles Act and Legal Framework
t: Under Section 185 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, a person is deemed to be driving under the influence of alcohol if blood alcohol exceeds:
e: Section 185 sets the limit at 30 mg of alcohol per 100 ml of blood detected by a breath analyser or other test. Own damage claims arising while driving under the influence are excluded from the policy.

topic: Motor Vehicles Act and Legal Framework
t: Which section of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 deals with the duty of insurers to satisfy judgments and awards against persons insured in respect of third party risks?
e: After the 2019 amendment the former Section 149 was renumbered as Section 150; it binds the insurer to satisfy awards against the insured, subject to limited statutory defences, once notice of the proceedings has been given.

topic: Motor Vehicles Act and Legal Framework
t: Under Section 196 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (as amended in 2019), driving an uninsured vehicle is punishable for a first offence with:
o: Imprisonment up to 3 months or fine up to ₹2,000 or both
Imprisonment up to 6 months or fine up to ₹5,000 or both
e: The amended Section 196 prescribes imprisonment up to three months, or fine up to ₹2,000, or both for a first offence, and up to three months or ₹4,000 or both for subsequent offences.

topic: Motor Vehicles Act and Legal Framework
t: Under Section 50 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, on sale of a vehicle within the same State the transferee must report the transfer to the registering authority within:
e: Section 50 requires the transferor to report within 14 days and the transferee to apply within 30 days for a transfer within the State; where the vehicle moves to another State the transferee has 45 days.

topic: Motor Vehicles Act and Legal Framework
t: Under Section 164 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (as amended in 2019), the no-fault compensation payable in case of death of a victim is:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Section 164 provides ₹5 lakh for death and ₹2.5 lakh for grievous hurt without the claimant having to prove negligence. It replaced the earlier Section 140 (₹50,000 / ₹25,000) and Section 163A.

topic: Motor Vehicles Act and Legal Framework
t: Under Section 2(21) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, a 'light motor vehicle' is one whose gross vehicle weight or unladen weight does not exceed:
e: A light motor vehicle is a transport or non-transport vehicle with gross vehicle weight (or unladen weight for non-transport) not exceeding 7,500 kg. The Supreme Court in Mukund Dewangan (2017), affirmed in 2024, held an LMV licence holder may drive a transport vehicle of that weight class.

topic: Types of Motor Vehicles and Policies
t: Which of the following is NOT a section of the standard Private Car Package Policy?
o: Section IV – Loss of personal belongings of passengers
Section I – Loss of or damage to the vehicle insured
Section II – Liability to third parties
Section III – Personal accident cover for owner-driver
e: The package policy has three sections: own damage, third party liability and personal accident to owner-driver. Personal belongings cover is not a standard section, though it may be offered as an add-on.

topic: Types of Motor Vehicles and Policies
t: Under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, a 'stage carriage' is:
o: A vehicle carrying passengers for hire as a whole under a single contract
A motor vehicle carrying more than six passengers for hire or reward at separate fares paid by or for individual passengers for the journey or stages of it
A goods vehicle plying between fixed stages
A school bus owned by an educational institution
e: Section 2(40) defines a stage carriage as one carrying more than six passengers (excluding driver) for hire or reward at separate fares; a contract carriage is hired as a whole under one contract.

topic: Types of Motor Vehicles and Policies
t: A two-wheeler package policy provides third party property damage cover up to:
e: For two-wheelers the TPPD limit under the policy is ₹1 lakh, while private cars and commercial vehicles carry ₹7.5 lakh. The insured may restrict TPPD to the statutory ₹6,000 for a small premium discount.

topic: Types of Motor Vehicles and Policies
t: Under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, a 'maxi cab' is a motor vehicle constructed or adapted to carry, excluding the driver:
o: More than 6 but not more than 12 passengers
e: Section 2(22) defines a maxi cab as carrying more than six but not more than twelve passengers excluding the driver, for hire or reward; a motor cab carries up to six.

t: Which of the following is NOT a rating factor for own damage premium of a private car?
e: OD premium is based on IDV, cubic capacity, age of vehicle and the zone (Zone A metros and Zone B rest of India). Personal factors such as marital status are not used in Indian motor rating.

t: For a vintage car certified by the Vintage and Classic Car Club of India, the discount allowed on own damage premium is:
e: A vintage car (manufactured before 31 December 1940 and certified as such) enjoys a 25% discount on OD premium in recognition of its limited, careful use.

topic: Third Party Liability Claims and MACT
t: An appeal against an award of a Motor Accident Claims Tribunal lies to the High Court under Section 173 within:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Section 173 allows appeal to the High Court within 90 days of the award. No appeal lies if the amount in dispute is less than ₹1 lakh, and the appellant must deposit ₹25,000 or 50% of the award, whichever is less.

t: Electrical and electronic fittings not part of the manufacturer's standard fitment are insured at an additional own damage premium of:
e: Non-standard electrical/electronic accessories (music systems, extra lamps etc.) are covered by endorsement at 4% of their declared value. The same 4% rate applies to the value of CNG/LPG kits, plus ₹60 for third party liability.

t: An insured earns NCB of 25% on his car. He sells the car and buys a new one, insuring it within the prescribed period. Which is correct?
o: NCB can be transferred to the new vehicle because NCB belongs to the insured, not the vehicle
NCB lapses because the vehicle has changed
NCB passes to the buyer of the old car
NCB is reduced to 20% on the new vehicle
e: NCB is earned by the insured and follows him to a substituted vehicle of the same class. The buyer of the old car cannot inherit the seller's NCB, except legal heirs on death of the insured.

t: A private car's OD premium is ₹12,000 before NCB. The insured has had 3 consecutive claim-free years. The OD premium payable after NCB is:
e: Three claim-free years entitle the insured to 35% NCB. ₹12,000 less 35% (₹4,200) = ₹7,800. NCB applies only to the OD premium, not to TP premium.

t: A proposer who is a member of the Automobile Association of India (AAI) is entitled to a discount on OD premium of:
o: 5% subject to a maximum of ₹200 for private cars
e: AAI members receive 5% discount on OD premium subject to a maximum of ₹200 for private cars and ₹50 for two-wheelers.

t: In the private car package policy, which of the following is NOT one of the named own damage perils?
e: Section I lists perils such as fire, theft, riot, earthquake, flood, accidental external means, malicious act, terrorism, transit and landslide. Mechanical and electrical breakdown is expressly excluded.

t: Under the own damage section, damage to tyres and tubes is payable only if:
o: The tyres are less than one year old
The vehicle is damaged at the same time, in which case 50% of the replacement cost is paid
The tyres were purchased from an authorised dealer
The damage is caused by flood
e: Damage to tyres and tubes alone is excluded; where the insured vehicle is also damaged at the same time, the insurer's liability for tyres and tubes is limited to 50% of the cost of replacement.

t: The 'certificate of insurance' under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 is:
o: A statutory document in the prescribed form evidencing that a policy complying with Chapter XI exists
The proposal form signed by the insured
e: Section 147(3) provides that a policy is of no effect unless a certificate of insurance in the form prescribed under the Central Motor Vehicles Rules is issued. It must be produced to police on demand.

t: An annual OD premium of ₹15,000 was paid. The insurer cancels the package policy after 3 months because the insured sold the vehicle. The refund of OD premium is:
e: Cancellation initiated by the insurer attracts pro-rata refund of premium for the unexpired period: 9/12 × ₹15,000 = ₹11,250. Had the insured requested cancellation, short period scale (40% retained for 3 months) would apply, giving a refund of ₹9,000.

t: Which condition of the motor policy requires the insured to take all reasonable steps to safeguard the vehicle and keep it in efficient condition?
e: The 'reasonable care' condition obliges the insured to safeguard the vehicle from loss, maintain it in efficient condition, and allow the insurer to inspect it. Leaving a car unlocked with keys inside can breach this condition.

t: A painting bill of ₹30,000 is submitted as a consolidated amount without separating material and labour. How is depreciation applied?
o: 25% of the bill (₹7,500) is treated as paint material and 50% depreciation is applied on it, i.e. ₹3,750
e: When a consolidated painting bill is given, 25% of the total is deemed to be paint material, on which 50% depreciation applies. Here ₹7,500 × 50% = ₹3,750 is deducted; labour is paid in full.

topic: Types of Motor Vehicles and Policies
t: Following the Supreme Court direction of 2018, a new two-wheeler sold in India must be insured for third party liability for a minimum period of:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). From 1 September 2018 insurers must issue long-term third party cover of 5 years for new two-wheelers and 3 years for new private cars, as directed by the Supreme Court and implemented by IRDAI.

t: In a partial loss claim, which of the following items is NOT subject to depreciation under the standard private car policy?
e: Glass parts carry nil depreciation. Batteries and plastic parts attract 50%, fibre glass components 30%, and other parts age-based rates.

t: A 2-year-old car met with an accident. Metal parts ₹50,000 (depreciation 10%), plastic parts ₹8,000, labour ₹10,000, compulsory deductible ₹1,000. What is the payable claim?
e: Metal parts: ₹50,000 − 10% = ₹45,000; plastic parts: ₹8,000 − 50% = ₹4,000; labour ₹10,000 in full. Total ₹59,000 less deductible ₹1,000 = ₹58,000.

t: In Gurshinder Singh v. Shriram General Insurance (2020), the Supreme Court held that in a theft claim:
o: Delay in intimating the insurer is not fatal if the FIR was lodged promptly and the theft is genuine
Delay in intimating the insurer is always fatal to the claim
The insurer need not pay if the keys were not surrendered
Only 75% of IDV is payable on delayed intimation
e: The Court ruled that where the insured promptly reported the theft to the police and the loss is not in doubt, mere delay in informing the insurer cannot be a ground to repudiate the claim.

t: The insurer's 'right to repair' under the motor policy means that:
o: The insured must always repair at a garage of his choice
The insurer may at its option repair, reinstate or replace the vehicle or parts instead of paying cash
The insurer must repair within 7 days
The insurer bears consequential loss during repair
e: The policy gives the insurer the option to repair, reinstate or replace the vehicle or any part of it, or pay in cash the amount of loss, limited to the IDV. Consequential loss remains excluded.

t: Under IRDAI guidelines on 'non-standard' claims, where a goods vehicle was overloaded beyond its licensed carrying capacity at the time of accident, the OD claim is settled at:
e: Non-standard settlement guidelines allow payment of 75% of the admissible claim for breaches such as overloading or any other breach of warranty/condition, including limitation as to use, where the breach has no direct nexus with the loss.

t: A car with IDV ₹6,00,000 is badly damaged in a flood. The surveyor assesses repair cost at ₹4,80,000. How should the claim be treated?
o: As a partial loss, paying ₹4,80,000 less depreciation
As a constructive total loss since repair cost exceeds 75% of IDV
As a partial loss subject to 50% depreciation on all parts
e: Repair cost of ₹4,80,000 is 80% of IDV, exceeding the 75% CTL threshold, so the claim is settled on total loss basis at IDV less deductible, with salvage going to the insurer. Flood is a covered peril.

t: Deduction for health insurance premium under Section 80D for an individual below 60 years (self and family) is up to:
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). ₹25,000; ₹50,000 where the insured is a senior citizen; an additional ₹25,000/₹50,000 for parents.

topic: Third Party Liability Claims and MACT
t: In National Insurance Co. v. Swaran Singh (2004), the Supreme Court laid down that where the driver did not hold a valid licence, the insurer:
o: Can refuse payment outright to the third party
Is liable only for 50% of the award
Must pay only if the owner also had no knowledge
Must pay the third party and recover from the owner where breach is established
e: Swaran Singh established the 'pay and recover' principle: the insurer must satisfy the award to protect the innocent third party, and may recover from the insured if it proves the owner's wilful breach regarding the driver's licence.

topic: Third Party Liability Claims and MACT
t: Under Section 173 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, before an insurer can appeal against a Tribunal award of ₹8,00,000, it must deposit with the High Court:
e: The appellant must deposit ₹25,000 or 50% of the award, whichever is less. 50% of ₹8 lakh is ₹4 lakh, so the lower figure of ₹25,000 applies.

topic: Third Party Liability Claims and MACT
t: In National Insurance Co. v. Pranay Sethi (2017), the Supreme Court fixed the addition for 'future prospects' for a deceased salaried person below 40 years with a permanent job at:
e: Pranay Sethi set future prospects at 50% (below 40), 30% (40–50) and 15% (50–60) for permanent employees, and 40%, 25% and 10% for self-employed or fixed-salary persons in the same age bands.

topic: Third Party Liability Claims and MACT
t: Under Section 159 of the amended Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, the police officer must forward the accident information report to the Claims Tribunal within:
e: Section 159 requires the police to prepare and submit the accident information report to the Claims Tribunal within three months. Under Section 166(4) this report is treated as an application for compensation.

topic: Third Party Liability Claims and MACT
t: Which of the following persons can NOT ordinarily be treated as a 'third party' for a claim under the Act policy?
o: A pedestrian hit by the insured vehicle
The owner of goods travelling in the goods vehicle
The owner-insured himself who dies while driving his own vehicle
A passenger in another vehicle involved in the collision
e: The insured owner cannot be a third party to his own policy; his death while driving is covered only by the compulsory PA section. Pedestrians, occupants of other vehicles and owners of goods carried are third parties.

topic: Third Party Liability Claims and MACT
t: Rajesh, aged 32, salaried with a permanent job earning ₹30,000 per month, dies in an accident leaving a wife and two children. Using Pranay Sethi and Sarla Verma, the loss of dependency (before conventional heads) is approximately:
e: Annual income ₹3,60,000 + 50% future prospects = ₹5,40,000; deduct one-third for personal expenses (3 dependents) = ₹3,60,000; multiplier for age 31–35 is 16; ₹3,60,000 × 16 = ₹57,60,000.

topic: Third Party Liability Claims and MACT
t: Under Section 158 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, the driver of a vehicle involved in an accident must, on demand by a police officer, produce the certificate of insurance within:
e: Section 158 requires production of the certificate of insurance (and licence/registration) on demand, or at a police station within seven days of the accident if not immediately available.

topic: Add-on Covers, Regulations and Recent Developments
t: The 'Engine Protect' add-on cover typically pays for:
o: Damage to the engine and gearbox due to water ingression or leakage of lubricating oil following an insured peril
Wear and tear of engine parts due to ageing
e: Engine protect covers hydrostatic lock and consequential engine/gearbox damage from water ingress or oil leakage, which the base policy excludes as consequential or mechanical loss. Wear and tear remains excluded.

t: Third-party insurance is compulsory for a motor vehicle used in a public place under which section of the Motor Vehicles Act 1988?
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). Section 146 makes TP cover compulsory; Section 164 fixes no-fault compensation (₹5 lakh death / ₹2.5 lakh grievous hurt).

topic: Add-on Covers, Regulations and Recent Developments
t: In July 2022 IRDAI permitted insurers to introduce which of the following technology-enabled add-ons under own damage cover?
o: Pay as you drive and Pay how you drive
e: IRDAI allowed 'Pay as you drive' (usage-based) and 'Pay how you drive' (telematics-based) covers and floater policies for multiple vehicles of one owner, as add-ons to the basic OD policy.

topic: Add-on Covers, Regulations and Recent Developments
t: The 'Consumables' add-on in a motor package policy covers:
o: The cost of fuel during repair period
Items like engine oil, coolant, nuts, bolts, washers and grease consumed during accidental repair
e: The base policy does not pay for consumables used in repair; the add-on covers lubricants, coolants, brake oil, nuts, bolts, clips and similar items used while repairing accidental damage.

t: Under the IRDAI grievance redressal norms, an insurer should resolve a policyholder's grievance within:
e: The Protection of Policyholders' Interests framework requires acknowledgement within 3 working days and resolution within 2 weeks; unresolved grievances may be escalated to the Bima Bharosa portal or the Ombudsman.

t: Which of the following best describes 'telematics' in motor insurance?
o: Use of devices or mobile apps to capture driving behaviour and vehicle usage data for pricing and claims
e: Telematics uses OBD devices, GPS and smartphone sensors to record mileage, speed, braking and location, enabling usage-based pricing, accident reconstruction and theft tracing.

t: The VAHAN database maintained by the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways is useful to motor insurers mainly for:
o: Verifying registration details, ownership and insurance status of vehicles
e: VAHAN holds nationwide vehicle registration data; insurers upload policy details to it and use it to validate chassis/engine numbers and detect uninsured vehicles, reducing fraud at underwriting.
